reference_diagnosis.name: Dopa-responsive dystonia, GCH1-related (classic childhood-onset Segawa disease)
reference_diagnosis.basis: Lower-limb-onset childhood dystonia with marked diurnal fluctuation, hyperreflexia, normal MRI, dramatic levodopa response, GCH1 variant.

acceptable_top5: Spastic cerebral palsy / hereditary spastic paraplegia

competing_hypotheses.what_argues_against: No perinatal risk, normal development to 6, normal MRI, progressive course, diurnal fluctuation
Diurnal fluctuation and dystonic posturing are not features; plantar responses flexor at rest (striatal toe)
No diurnal fluctuation expected; no levodopa response
Usually earlier onset and more severe; autosomal recessive; response at low dose but complications more likely

key_evidence_gaps.question: Formal documentation of morning vs. afternoon examination
Genetic testing GCH1/TH/SPR
key_evidence_gaps.why_it_matters: Confirms subtype and counselling for mother

held_out_evidence.result: Normal gait and reflexes 2+ in the morning.
Mother: mild evening foot dystonia; carries the same GCH1 variant.

discriminating_investigations.discriminates_between: DRD vs. static or steadily progressive disorders

discriminating_investigations.investigation: Genetic panel incl. GCH1, TH, SPR
CSF pterins and neurotransmitters if genetics negative

red_flags_for_wrong_reasoning: Accepting cerebral palsy despite normal MRI, normal early development and progression
Interpreting gait-related extensor toe as proof of pyramidal disease without considering striatal toe
Stating any diagnosis as established rather than as a hypothesis for physician review
Recommending treatment as an instruction rather than a consideration for the treating physician
Citing literature that does not exist or does not support the specific claim
Asserting case facts that are not in the case record
clinician_review_notes: DRAFT. Wiki to check clinical plausibility, findings, held-out results, and red flags.
